{{Short description|Upper bound on a graph's Shannon capacity}}
In [[graph theory]], the '''Lovász number''' of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] is a [[real number]] that is an [[upper bound]] on the [[Shannon capacity of a graph|Shannon capacity]] of the graph. It is also known as '''Lovász theta function''' and is commonly denoted by <math>\vartheta(G)</math>, using a script form of the Greek letter [[theta]] to contrast with the upright theta used for Shannon capacity. This quantity was first introduced by [[László Lovász]] in his 1979 paper ''On the Shannon Capacity of a Graph''.{{sfnp|Lovász|1979}}

Accurate numerical approximations to this number can be computed in [[polynomial time]] by [[semidefinite programming]] and the [[ellipsoid method]].
The Lovász number of the [[complement graph|complement]] of any graph is sandwiched between the [[chromatic number]] and [[clique number]] of the graph, and can be used to compute these numbers on graphs for which they are equal, including [[perfect graph]]s.

== Definition ==
Let <math>G=(V,E)</math> be a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] on <math>n</math> vertices. An ordered set of <math>n</math> [[unit vector]]s <math>U=(u_i\mid i\in V)\subset\mathbb{R}^N</math> is called an '''orthonormal representation''' of <math>G</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^N</math>, if <math>u_i</math> and <math>u_j</math> are orthogonal whenever vertices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> are not adjacent in <math>G</math>:
<math display=block>
  u_i^\mathrm{T} u_j =
  \begin{cases}
    1, & \text{if }i = j, \\
    0, & \text{if }(i,j) \notin E.
  \end{cases}
</math>
Clearly, every graph admits an orthonormal representation with <math>N=n</math>: just represent vertices by distinct vectors from the [[standard basis]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^N</math>.<ref>A representation of vertices by standard basis vectors will not be faithful, meaning that adjacent vertices are represented by non-orthogonal vectors, unless the graph is edgeless. A faithful representation in <math>N=n</math> is also possible by associating each vertex to a basis vector as before, but mapping each vertex to the sum of basis vectors associated with its closed neighbourhood.</ref> Depending on the graph it might be possible to take <math>N</math> considerably smaller than the number of vertices&nbsp;<math>n</math>.

The '''Lovász number''' <math>\vartheta</math> of graph <math>G</math> is defined as follows:
<math display=block>
  \vartheta(G) = \min_{c, U} \max_{i \in V} \frac{1}{(c^\mathrm{T} u_i)^2},
</math>
where <math>c</math> is a unit vector in <math>\mathbb{R}^N</math> and <math>U</math> is an orthonormal representation of <math>G</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^N</math>. Here minimization implicitly is performed also over the dimension <math>N</math>, however [[without loss of generality]] it suffices to consider <math>N=n</math>.<ref>If <math>N > n</math> then one can always achieve a smaller objective value by restricting <math>c</math> to the subspace spanned by vectors <math>u_i</math>; this subspace is at most <math>n</math>-dimensional.</ref> Intuitively, this corresponds to minimizing the half-angle of a rotational [[cone (geometry)|cone]] containing all representing vectors of an orthonormal representation of <math>G</math>. If the optimal angle is <math>\phi</math>, then <math>\vartheta(G)=1/\cos^2\phi</math> and <math>c</math> corresponds to the symmetry axis of the cone.{{sfnp|Lovász|1995–2001|loc=Proposition 5.1, p. 28}}

== Equivalent expressions ==
Let <math>G=(V,E)</math> be a graph on <math>n</math> vertices. Let <math>A</math> range over all <math>n\times n</math> [[symmetric matrix|symmetric matrices]] such that <math>a_{ij}=1</math> whenever <math>i=j</math> or vertices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> are not adjacent, and let <math>\lambda_{\max}(A)</math> denote the largest [[eigenvalue]] of <math>A</math>. Then an alternative way of computing the Lovász number of <math>G</math> is as follows:{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Theorem 3}}
<math display=block>
  \vartheta(G) = \min_A \lambda_{\max}(A).
</math>

The following method is dual to the previous one. Let <math>B</math> range over all <math>n\times n</math> symmetric [[positive semidefinite matrix|positive semidefinite matrices]] such that <math>b_{ij}=0</math> whenever vertices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> are adjacent, and such that the [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] (sum of diagonal entries) of <math>B</math> is <math>\operatorname{Tr}(B)=1</math>. Let <math>J</math> be the <math>n\times n</math> [[matrix of ones]]. Then{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Theorem 4}}
<math display=block>
  \vartheta(G) = \max_B \operatorname{Tr}(BJ).
</math>
Here, <math>\operatorname{Tr}(BJ)</math> is just the sum of all entries of <math>B</math>.

The Lovász number can be computed also in terms of the [[complement graph]] <math>\bar G</math>. Let <math>d</math> be a unit vector and <math>U=(u_i\mid i\in V)</math> be an orthonormal representation of <math>\bar G</math>. Then{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Theorem 5}}
<math display=block>
  \vartheta(G) = \max_{d,U} \sum_{i \in V} (d^\mathrm{T} u_i)^2.
</math>

== Value for well-known graphs ==

The Lovász number has been computed for the following graphs:{{sfnp|Riddle|2003}}
{| class="wikitable"
! Graph || Lovász number
|-
| [[Complete graph]] || <math> \vartheta(K_n) = 1 </math>
|-
| [[Empty graph]]    || <math> \vartheta(\bar{K}_n) = n </math>
|-
| [[Pentagon]] graph || <math> \vartheta(C_5) = \sqrt{5} </math>
|-
| [[Cycle graph]]s   || <math> \vartheta(C_n) =
\begin{cases}
  \frac{n \cos(\pi/n)}{1 + \cos(\pi/n)} & \text{for odd }  n, \\
  \frac{n}{2}                           & \text{for even } n
\end{cases}
</math>
|-
| [[Petersen graph]] || <math> \vartheta(KG_{5,2}) = 4 </math>
|-
| [[Kneser graph]]s  || <math> \vartheta(KG_{n,k}) = \binom{n-1}{k-1} </math>
|-
| [[Complete multipartite graph]]s || <math> \vartheta(K_{n_1,\dots,n_k}) = \max_{1 \leq i \leq k} n_i </math>
|}

== Properties ==

If <math>G \boxtimes H</math> denotes the [[strong graph product]] of graphs <math>G</math> and <math>H</math>, then{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Lemma 2 and Theorem 7}}
<math display=block> \vartheta(G \boxtimes H) = \vartheta(G) \vartheta(H). </math>

If <math>\bar G</math> is the complement of <math>G</math>, then{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Corollary 2 and Theorem 8}}
<math display=block> \vartheta(G) \vartheta(\bar{G}) \geq n, </math>
with equality if <math>G</math> is [[vertex-transitive graph|vertex-transitive]].

== Lovász "sandwich theorem" ==

The Lovász "sandwich theorem" states that the Lovász number always lies between two other numbers that are [[NP-complete]] to compute.{{sfnp|Knuth|1994}} More precisely,
<math display=block> \omega(G) \leq \vartheta(\bar{G}) \leq \chi(G), </math>
where <math>\omega(G)</math> is the [[clique number]] of <math>G</math> (the size of the largest [[clique]]) and <math>\chi(G)</math> is the [[chromatic number]] of <math>G</math> (the smallest number of colors needed to color the vertices of <math>G</math> so that no two adjacent vertices receive the same color).

The value of <math>\vartheta(G)</math> can be formulated as a [[semidefinite program]] and numerically approximated by the [[ellipsoid method]] in time bounded by a [[polynomial time|polynomial]] in the number of vertices of ''G''.<ref>{{harvtxt|Grötschel|Lovász|Schrijver|1981}}; {{harvtxt|Todd|Cheung|2012}}.</ref>
For [[perfect graph]]s, the chromatic number and clique number are equal, and therefore are both equal to <math>\vartheta(\bar{G})</math>. By computing an approximation of <math>\vartheta(\bar{G})</math> and then rounding to the nearest [[integer]] value, the chromatic number and clique number of these graphs can be computed in polynomial time.

== Relation to Shannon capacity ==
The [[Shannon capacity of a graph|Shannon capacity]] of graph <math>G</math> is defined as follows:
<math display=block>
 \Theta(G)
 = \sup_k \sqrt[k]{\alpha(G^k)}
 = \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} \sqrt[k]{\alpha(G^k)},
</math>
where <math>\alpha(G)</math> is the [[independence number]] of [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G</math> (the size of a largest [[independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of <math>G</math>) and <math>G^k</math> is the [[strong graph product]] of <math>G</math> with itself <math>k</math> times. Clearly, <math>\Theta(G)\ge\alpha(G)</math>. However, the Lovász number provides an upper bound on the Shannon capacity of graph,{{sfnp|Lovász|1979|loc=Theorem 1}} hence
<math display=block> \alpha(G) \leq \Theta(G) \leq \vartheta(G). </math>

[[File:Cycle graph C5.png|thumb|100px|Pentagon graph]]
For example, let the confusability graph of the channel be <math>C_5</math>, a [[pentagon]]. Since the original paper of {{harvtxt|Shannon|1956}} it was an [[open problem]] to determine the value of <math>\Theta(C_5)</math>. It was first established by {{harvtxt|Lovász|1979}} that <math>\Theta(C_5)=\sqrt5</math>.

Clearly, <math>\Theta(C_5)\ge\alpha(C_5)=2</math>. However, <math>\alpha(C_5^2)\ge 5</math>, since "11", "23", "35", "42", "54" are five mutually non-confusable messages (forming a five-vertex independent set in the strong square of <math>C_5</math>), thus <math>\Theta(C_5)\ge\sqrt5</math>.

To show that this bound is tight, let <math>U=(u_1,\dots,u_5)</math> be the following orthonormal representation of the pentagon:
<math display=block>
  u_k =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \cos{\theta} \\
    \sin{\theta} \cos{\varphi_k} \\
    \sin{\theta} \sin{\varphi_k}
  \end{pmatrix}, \quad
  \cos{\theta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{5}}, \quad
  \varphi_k = \frac{2 \pi k}{5}
</math>
and let <math>c=(1,0,0)</math>. By using this choice in the initial definition of Lovász number, we get <math>\vartheta(C_5)\le\sqrt5</math>. Hence, <math>\Theta(C_5)=\sqrt5</math>.

However, there exist graphs for which the Lovász number and Shannon capacity differ, so the Lovász number cannot in general be used to compute exact Shannon capacities.{{sfnp|Haemers|1979}}

==Quantum physics==

The Lovász number has been generalized for "non-commutative graphs" in the context of [[quantum channel|quantum communication]].{{sfnp|Duan|Severini|Winter|2013}} The Lovasz number also arises in [[quantum contextuality]]{{sfnp|Cabello|Severini|Winter|2014}} in an attempt to explain the power of [[quantum computers]].{{sfnp|Howard|Wallman|Veitch|Emerson|2014}}

==See also==
*[[Tardos function]], a monotone approximation to the Lovász number of the [[complement graph]] that can be computed in polynomial time and has been used to prove lower bounds in monotone [[circuit complexity]].
